key_facts: Searching algorithms are designed to check for or retrieve an element from a data structure, and are classified into two categories: Sequential Search and Interval Search.
Linear Search starts from the leftmost element of the list, compares the target x with each element one by one, returning the index if matched or -1 if no element matches.
Interval Search algorithms are specifically designed for searching in sorted data structures.
The hash table section covers basic concepts, direct-address tables, hash tables, hash functions, and open addressing as a collision-resolution technique.

The document is authored by Tran Ngoc Bao Duy from the Faculty of Computer Science and Engineering, Ho Chi Minh University of Technology, VNU-HCM, as Chapter 7 of a Data Structures and Algorithms course.
generated_text: Introduction to Searching and Hashing Welcome to our lesson on Searching Algorithms and Hash Tables. In this section, we will explore fundamental techniques for finding and retrieving elements within data structures. We'll begin by examining two primary categories of searching algorithms and then move on to the core concepts of hash tables and hash functions. Topics Covered Searching Algorithms: Sequential Search and Interval Search Hash Tables: Basic concepts, including Hash Functions like the Division Method 1. Searching Algorithms Searching Algorithms are designed to check for an element or retrieve an element from any data structure where it is stored. Based on the type of search operation, these algorithms are generally classified into two categories. Sequential Search In a sequential search, the list or array is traversed sequentially, and every element is checked one by one. A common example is the Linear Search. Linear Search Approach Start from the leftmost element of the list and, one by one, compare the target element x with each element of the list. If x matches an element, return its index. If x doesn’t match any of the elements after checking them all, return -1. The time complexity of the Linear Search algorithm is O(n) . Interval Search These algorithms are specifically designed for searching in sorted data structures. They are generally more efficient than sequential searches because they repeatedly target intervals where the search element might be. Interpolation Search Interpolation Search is an improvement over Binary Search for instances where the values in a sorted array are uniformly distributed. Approach: Calculate the value of pos using the probe position formula. pos = lo + ((x - arr[lo]) * (hi - lo)) / (arr[hi] - arr[lo]) Where: arr is the array, x is the element to be searched, lo is the starting index, and hi is the ending index. If it is a match, return the index of the item and exit. If the item is less than arr[pos], calculate the probe position of the left sub-array. Otherwise, calculate the same in the right sub-array. Repeat until a match is found or the sub-array reduces to zero. Time Complexity: If elements are uniformly distributed, the complexity is O(log log n) . In the worst case, it can take up to O(n) . 2. Hash Tables and Hash Functions Hash tables are a fundamental data structure used for efficient data retrieval. They rely on hash functions to map keys to specific locations, or slots, within the table. The Division Method A common technique for creating hash functions is the division method. Definition: In the division method, we map a key k into one of m slots by taking the remainder of k divided by m . The hash function is: h(k) = k mod m Example: If the hash table has size m = 12 and the key is k = 100 , then the hash value is h(100) = 100 mod 12 = 4. The key k would be mapped to slot 4. Choosing a good value for m: m should not be a power of 2. m should be a prime number not too close to an exact power of 2. Summary In this lesson, we defined searching algorithms and explored two main types. Sequential Search , like Linear Search, checks every element and has a time complexity of O(n). Interval Search , like Interpolation Search, is designed for sorted data and can be much faster, with an average time complexity of O(log log n) for uniformly distributed data. We also introduced the concept of Hash Functions , focusing on the Division Method (h(k) = k mod m) as a way to map keys to indices in a hash table.
